qs.q: A patient presents with high gastric acid production stimulated via the vagus nerve. Which specific receptor does acetylcholine bind to on parietal cells to achieve this?
qs.e: Acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve binds to M3 muscarinic receptors to increase intracellular calcium and activate the proton pump. H2 receptors are instead activated by histamine.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitter released by the vagus nerve binds directly to M3 muscarinic receptors to increase intracellular calcium and stimulate gastric acid secretion?
qs.e: Acetylcholine is released by the vagus nerve and binds to M3 muscarinic receptors to activate the proton pump via calcium. Histamine acts via H2 receptors and cAMP rather than M3 muscarinic receptors.
qs.s: Gastric Acid Secretion and Thyroid Disorders: MCQs

qs.q: Damage to the vagus nerve would most directly impair which phase of gastric secretion?
qs.e: The cephalic phase of gastric secretion is entirely mediated by vagal nerve stimulation (long reflex) in response to sensory inputs like the sight, smell, or thought of food. While the vagus nerve also influences the gastric phase (e.g., via gastrin release), damage would most directly and significantly impair the cephalic phase, which prepares the stomach for incoming food. ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The vagus nerve (CN X) is the longest cranial nerve, extending from the medulla to the abdomen. It carries parasympathetic fibers to thoraco‑abdominal viscera and conveys sensory information from the gut and heart.

sections.p: The vagus is a mixed motor‑sensory nerve that provides the main parasympathetic outflow to the heart, lungs, and most of the gastrointestinal tract.
b: Originates in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus in the medulla
Travels within the carotid sheath bilaterally

sections.p: After exiting the jugular foramen, the nerve descends in the neck, gives off the superior laryngeal branch, then continues into the thorax and abdomen.
b: Superior laryngeal, recurrent laryngeal, cardiac, pulmonary, and esophageal branches
Forms the anterior vagal trunk on the right and posterior trunk on the left after the esophageal hiatus

sections.p: In the neck it lies between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery; in the thorax it runs posterior to the root of the lung and anterior to the aortic arch.
b: Close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the aortic arch
Accompanies the thoracic duct in the posterior mediastinum

sections.p: Arterial branches from the ascending pharyngeal, superior thyroid, and posterior auricular arteries supply the cervical portion; thoracic branches arise from the bronchial and esophageal arteries.
b: Vascular supply mirrors its course, ensuring perfusion for autonomic fibers

sections.p: Motor fibers arise from the dorsal motor nucleus; sensory fibers from the nucleus of the solitary tract; visceral afferents travel with the vagus to the nucleus tractus solitarius.
b: Parasympathetic pre‑ganglionic fibers synapse in intramural ganglia of target organs

sections.p: Provides parasympathetic tone to lower heart rate, stimulate gastric acid and motility, and modulate inflammation via the cholinergic anti‑inflammatory pathway.
b: Acetylcholine release at SA node → M2 receptors → bradycardia
Stimulates gastric secretions; hypoglycemia increases vagal activity

sections.p: Vagal dysfunction can cause dysphagia, hoarseness, tachycardia, gastroparesis, or abnormal heart rate variability. Lesions may be traumatic, iatrogenic, or infectious.
b: Vagal neuropathy in diabetes or HIV → gastroparesis
Vagus involvement in prion‑like spread of α‑synuclein from gut to brain

t.b: Does autonomic balance favor parasympathetic tone? Low HRV suggests vagal impairment and higher cardiovascular risk

t.b: Is gastric motility delayed? Delayed emptying supports vagal neuropathy
Is vocal cord movement reduced? Confirms recurrent laryngeal involvement

sections.p: Know the course, key branches, and how loss of vagal tone manifests clinically.
b: Vagus supplies the larynx; injury → hoarseness
Vagus mediates the cough reflex; lesions blunt cough

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dysphagia or aspiration leading to respiratory failure
Acute gastroparesis causing vomiting and electrolyte loss

faq.q: Why does vagal stimulation lower heart rate?
faq.a: Acetylcholine released at the SA node binds M2 receptors, increasing potassium conductance and slowing pacemaker activity.

faq.q: What causes a hoarse voice after thyroid surgery?
faq.a: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, which innervates the vocal cords.

faq.q: How can the vagus contribute to neurodegenerative disease?
faq.a: Pathogenic proteins can travel from the gut enteric nervous system via the vagus to the brainstem, seeding disease.
